parts.note: a sharp offshoot of poultry is the spur on a cockerel's leg, and The Poultry is itself a City of London ..., so the answer is another London ...

explanation.surface: A question about some sharp growth branching off from a farmyard of hens.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T on 'The Poultry' gives it away: Poultry is a street in the City of London. COCKSPUR STREET runs off Trafalgar Square in London, and a cockspur is the sharp spur on a cock's leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A cock's spur is literally a pointed outgrowth on a bird, and the full name belongs to a road near Trafalgar Square.

parts.note: read 'playful' as 'full of plays': a William who wrote many stage comedies

explanation.surface: A mischievous boy called William.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playful' suggests a frisky child, but it means a writer of plays: William Congreve wrote Restoration comedies such as The Way of the World.
explanation.definitionFit: The Restoration dramatist whose first name was William produced many comic stage works, making him full of plays.

parts.note: 'ditto' repeats the previous clue's William, and the pugnacious William is the one who invaded England in 1066

explanation.surface: Another fighting one, the same again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditto' refers back to William in 1-down; the warlike William is William the Conqueror.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norman duke William won the Battle of Hastings and so earned the epithet of a victor by force.

parts.note: the phrase 'pure and simple' hides two set names

explanation.surface: Just a man, nothing more to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pure and simple' looks like an idiom meaning 'nothing but', but both words attach to the same first name: Simon Pure, the genuine article from Centlivre's play, and Simple Simon of the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a man's first name that is paired with both 'Pure' and 'Simple' in well-known expressions.

clue.text: Trunk emptied, brush and comb not found in it ?

indicators.note: 'in it' says the letters sit inside the words of the phrase 'Trunk emptied' just read

explanation.surface: Someone unpacks a trunk and finds their brush and comb missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'trUNK EMPTied'. The definition describes hair that brush and comb have not touched.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair that has never met a brush or comb is untidy and dishevelled.

definitions.meaning: a seaboard is the coast, and the opposite is high inland country
a plateau is a raised stretch of level ground

explanation.surface: Someone names the reverse of a coastline and remarks how flat it is.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'seaboard' as SEA + BOARD: the opposite of sea is land and a board is a table, so the answer is the flip of the clue word as well as a flat plateau.
explanation.definitionFit: An elevated plain lies inland away from the coast and is level on top.

definitions.meaning: to urge someone is to spur them on
a curate eating his famously mixed breakfast egg with a spoon may end up with some of it on him

explanation.surface: Someone asks a soppy young clergyman to press ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The curate's egg is the proverbial egg that was good in parts; a clumsy, spoony curate has it on his face or clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To spur someone on is to incite them, and a messy eater has yolk stuck to him.

clue.text: Such port, the unusual pleasure of it goes to your head

parts.note: a treat is an unusual or special pleasure

indicators.note: the head of the word 'your' is its first letter

explanation.surface: Port wine so rare a pleasure that it goes straight to your head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' suggests the drink, but a treaty port was a harbour opened to foreign trade by treaty, as in China.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty port was a harbour thrown open to foreign merchants under an international agreement.

clue.text: Peer about the pub for George, so called

indicators.note: 'about' says the peering word goes round the word for the pub

parts.note: to peer is to pry, look closely
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A nobleman hanging around the local pub, known as George.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a lord but is the verb. Prinny was the nickname of George IV when Prince Regent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prince Regent, later George IV, was popularly nicknamed this.

clue.text: The question of tips does not concern him

definitions.text: The question of tips does not concern him

parts.words: The question of tips does not concern him
parts.note: the tips are cigarette tips, filter or plain, which matter nothing to someone who never lights up

explanation.surface: Someone untroubled by whether or how much to tip a waiter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' suggests gratuities, but it means cigarette tips: cork, filter or plain.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who never lights cigarettes has no interest in what kind of filter they carry.

clue.text: On the rails never the Colonel, of course!

definitions.text: On the rails never the Colonel, of course!

parts.words: On the rails never the Colonel, of course
parts.note: on the railway the word means a wheeled undercarriage, while on the golf course Colonel Bogey stands for par play; the clue contrasts the two

explanation.surface: Someone insists the Colonel always stays on the straight and narrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rails' suggests behaving well, but means railways, where a bogie is a pivoting wheel truck. 'Of course' hints at a golf course and the imaginary golfer Colonel Bogey.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway truck's swivelling wheel frame bears this name, spelt differently from the golfing Colonel.

clue.text: Port makes one dissolute to a point

parts.note: a roué is a dissolute man, a rake
N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A harbour town that turns a man into a debauchee.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'point' in crosswords is often a compass point: N, S, E or W.
explanation.definitionFit: The Normandy city on the Seine is a river harbour reachable by seagoing ships.

parts.note: something that grows in a pod and is fed to apes and other primates, a peanut

explanation.surface: An ape is described as having something pod-like.
explanation.walkthrough: The peanut grows in a pod and is the classic food thrown to apes at the zoo.
explanation.definitionFit: The peanut is a legume in a pod, popularly given to apes in zoos.

clue.text: It borders Canada and ends in it

definitions.text: It borders Canada and ends in it

parts.words: It borders Canada and ends in it
parts.note: a US state along the Canadian frontier whose postal abbreviation is its own first and last letters

explanation.surface: A place lying along the Canadian border, where things finish.
explanation.walkthrough: The state's postal code VT is made of its first and last letters, so its ends are found in it.
explanation.definitionFit: This New England state lies along the frontier with Quebec.

parts.note: Irene is the Greek goddess of peace; her emblem is the olive branch, and a pedigree is a family tree

explanation.surface: Asking about a woman called Irene's ancestry.
explanation.walkthrough: Irene reads as a woman's name but is Eirene, Greek goddess of peace, whose symbol is the olive branch; her family tree is an olive tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The olive is the emblem of peace, so the peace goddess's family tree would be this tree.

clue.text: Robert Lynd writing about the Orient being in a ferment

indicators.note: 'about' says the writer's signature goes round the word for the Orient

parts.note: the essayist Robert Lynd wrote under the pen name Y.Y.
the Orient is the East

explanation.surface: An essayist writing about Asia while himself in a ferment.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Lynd, the Irish essayist, signed his New Statesman pieces Y.Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Something frothing and fermenting behaves like dough working with leaven.

parts.note: read 'hell to' as 'add HELL to': these slow reptiles plus that word make the name of a butterfly

explanation.surface: Something that torments a butterfly.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a complaint, but adding HELL to these reptiles gives tortoiseshell, a butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: The shelled reptiles, joined to 'hell', name the tortoiseshell butterfly.

definitions.meaning: sleeping partners are investors who take no active part in a business
on a railway the rails sit in iron chairs fixed to the wooden beams beneath

explanation.surface: A couple dozing off beneath the furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chairs' are railway chairs, the iron fittings holding rails to the cross-beams under them.
explanation.definitionFit: Inactive business partners are called sleeping, and railway cross-ties carry the rail chairs.

parts.note: read literally, someone who employs a model, as a painter employs a sitter

explanation.surface: A firm that treats its staff exemplarily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model employer' is an idiom for a good boss, but here it is someone who hires a model to sit for them.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter hires sitters to pose, so they literally employ models.

clue.text: Puts one pound into Amsterdam exports

indicators.note: 'Puts ... into' tells us to make the letters into something new, rearranging them

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: Someone invests a pound in goods shipped out of Amsterdam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' signals that PUTS with I and L is made into a new arrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Netherlands is famous for exporting bulb flowers.

clue.text: Lee side the opposite of this

definitions.text: Lee side the opposite of this

parts.words: Lee side the opposite of this
parts.note: Lee is the Confederate general of the American Civil War, and the side opposing his was the Union

explanation.surface: A sailor contrasting the sheltered side with its opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lee side' sounds nautical, but it is General Robert E. Lee's side, the Confederates; their opponents were the Union forces.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US Civil War the Union government's troops fought the Confederacy.

clue.text: A swindler never short of notes

definitions.meaning: someone who fiddles is a cheat
a violinist always has musical notes to play

explanation.surface: A con man who always has banknotes in his pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' suggests banknotes, fitting the swindler, but they are musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheat is said to fiddle, and a violinist plays a fiddle full of musical tones.

clue.text: Forgers have a joint field in London

definitions.meaning: forgers here are metalworkers who work at a forge

definitions.text: have a joint field in London
definitions.meaning: joined to the word 'field' they make Smithfield, the London meat market

explanation.surface: Counterfeiters sharing a plot of land in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forgers' suggests counterfeiters but means blacksmiths; with 'field' joined on they give Smithfield, the London meat market.
explanation.definitionFit: People who work metal at a forge are blacksmiths.

indicators.note: 'thus' says the letters of the following words, rearranged this way, give the answer

explanation.surface: Someone was amazed at how to dig in clay soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thus' points to an anagram of DELVE MARL.
explanation.definitionFit: To have wondered at something is to have been amazed by it.

parts.note: a rising is an insurrection, so a man of the rising takes up arms against authority

explanation.surface: A man on his way up in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A rising man' sounds like someone going places, but a rising is a revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who joins an uprising is an insurgent.

parts.note: both a surgeon's slender instrument for exploring a wound and an investigation

explanation.surface: A question put to a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a surgical instrument and an investigation.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon's exploring instrument shares its name with a searching investigation.

parts.note: Paris here is the Trojan prince, embraced by his father, the king of Troy

explanation.surface: A king whose army captured the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took Paris' suggests a conquest of the city, but the King of Troy took his son Paris in his arms.
explanation.definitionFit: The last king of Troy fathered Paris, so could hold him in his arms.

parts.note: in Macaulay's poem Horatius prays 'O ...! father ...!' before swimming the river

explanation.surface: A man who was a parent to a Roman hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Horatius, in Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome, calls the river of Rome 'father' as he leaps in.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaulay's Horatius addresses Rome's river as his father in prayer.

clue.text: Straw that sounds agreeable to Bottom ?

indicators.note: 'that sounds' tells us to listen to the words that follow

parts.note: pally is friendly or agreeable, and Bottom in A Midsummer Night's Dream is turned into an ass

explanation.surface: Straw that seems pleasing to someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom is the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream given an ass's head; 'pally ass' said aloud is a straw mattress.
explanation.definitionFit: A palliasse is a mattress stuffed with straw, so the filling stands for the bed.

definitions.meaning: argentine means silvery, of the precious white metal
Long John is the ship's cook in Treasure Island

explanation.surface: A ship's cook from Argentina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Argentine' suggests Argentina but is the adjective for silver; Long John Silver is the sea-cook in Treasure Island.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective argentine derives from the Latin for this metal, and Stevenson's pirate cook bears it as surname.

definitions.meaning: the propositions set out in order from which a syllogism draws its conclusion

explanation.surface: Buildings arranged in sensible order.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses come from property and from logic, where a syllogism has major and minor propositions.
explanation.definitionFit: A business's property is so called, and in logic the propositions leading to a conclusion carry the same name.
